description: My background spans Data Science, Information Technology (IT), Computational and Applied Geophysics, Remote Sensing, Geographic Information Systems (GIS), and Geology, with specialized expertise in seismic interferometry and multidimensional tomographic imaging (2D, 3D, and 4D).Following my academic research experience, I transitioned into the Space & Defence sector.
summary:
I built NISAR Observatory, an interactive application that uses real NASA–ISRO radar data to track and visualize changes on Earth. Users can select a study area, find compatible observations, and download just the portion they need. Seven documented examples cover flooding, wetland inundation, wildfire-related change, land subsidence, earthquakes, volcanic activity and glacier motion.

The app’s main feature is its modular workflow. Users can load an example as editable steps, change a setting, compare the results and save or share the recipe. In Chókwè, Mozambique, changing one radar brightness threshold reduced the area flagged as potential new water from 90.47 to 51.40 km² using the same observations. The side-by-side maps show how a single processing decision shapes the result.

I built the application with Python, FastAPI, JavaScript and Leaflet. My goal was to make radar analysis approachable for students and the public while giving researchers and resource managers a repeatable way to examine changes, understand uncertainty and identify areas for follow-up.
details:
I developed NISAR Observatory to make NASA–ISRO radar observations easier to explore, interpret and turn into repeatable studies. The app lets users select an area and dates, find compatible NISAR L-band observations, and work with full downloads, smaller area subsets or local files. Its seven tools cover flooding, wetland inundation, wildfire-related surface change, land subsidence, earthquake deformation, volcanic surface change and glacier motion.

What makes it creative

Every documented example can become an editable workflow. Users can open a recorded result, inspect its processing steps, change a parameter and compare the new result with the original. They can also build a workflow from scratch, save it in My Tools, or export it as a JSON recipe for someone else to repeat or adapt.

In the Chókwè flood case, I changed one setting: the HH radar brightness threshold, from −17 to −18 dB. With the same two satellite observations and the same analysis grid, the area flagged as potential new water fell from 90.47 to 51.40 km². The side-by-side maps make the effect of that decision visible and give users a concrete way to explore how sensitive a result is to its settings.

Benefits and intended impact

I wanted beginners to be able to start with a real case and understand what the map shows. The Mission Library explains how radar measurements work, and each tutorial documents its inputs, reference evidence and limitations. Linked maps, time exploration and quality layers help users investigate change. PNG maps, numeric GeoTIFFs and self-contained HTML reports let them carry the results into presentations, GIS tools or further discussion. Educators can use the same workflow to teach radar interpretation, while researchers and resource managers can use it to identify areas for follow-up and document how they reached a result.

Technology and design considerations

I developed and tested the app on macOS. It runs locally with a Python and FastAPI backend and an HTML, CSS and JavaScript interface. It uses h5py to read NISAR files, NumPy and SciPy for scientific processing, Rasterio and pyproj for geospatial operations, and Leaflet and Plotly for maps and charts.

I designed around three practical needs: keeping downloads manageable, making analyses reproducible, and explaining what the evidence supports. The app offers area subsets, records the source observations and processing settings, and makes gaps in coverage and measurement limits visible alongside the maps.
